reason: The sources contain over a dozen well-documented, multi-sourced facts supporting a compelling narrative about the start of uninterrupted human occupation in space.
story: On October 31, 2000, three spacefarers—former U.S. Navy SEAL Bill Shepherd and Russian cosmonauts Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev—launched from Baikonur aboard a Soyuz rocket. Two days later, on November 2, 2000, they docked with the International Space Station and floated inside, opening a landmark chapter in spaceflight. At the time, the station consisted of just three main modules, so power-starved that one module was left unheated. Shepherd invoked naval tradition and insisted on calling their outpost Alpha. During their 136-day stay, the trio unpacked supplies, activated life support systems, and hosted visiting space shuttles that delivered massive solar arrays and the Destiny laboratory module. By the time they handed control over to Expedition 2 and returned home aboard Space Shuttle Discovery in March 2001, they had established an unbroken streak of human orbital habitation that continues to this day.
angle: Humanity has maintained an unbroken chain of continuous living in space every single day since Expedition 1 boarded the ISS on November 2, 2000.

claims.claim: Expedition 1 was the first long-duration resident crew to live aboard the International Space Station.
The Expedition 1 crew consisted of three members: American commander William Shepherd and Russian cosmonauts Yuri Gidzenko and Sergei Krikalev.
The crew launched on October 31, 2000, aboard a Soyuz TM-31 spacecraft from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.
The Soyuz spacecraft docked with the International Space Station on November 2, 2000, allowing the crew to enter the station.
Commander William Shepherd was a former U.S. Navy SEAL before becoming a NASA astronaut.
Flight engineer Sergei Krikalev had previously flown to the station on mission STS-88 in 1998, making him the first person to visit the ISS twice.
Expedition 1 established an unbroken streak of continuous human presence in orbit that has lasted every day since November 2, 2000.
Commander Shepherd requested the use of the radio call sign Alpha for the station and crew, citing naval tradition.
Space Shuttle Endeavour visited the station on mission STS-97 in December 2000, delivering its first pair of large U.S. solar arrays.
Space Shuttle Atlantis delivered the US $1.4 billion Destiny research module to the station during mission STS-98 in February 2001.
The Expedition 1 crew spent 136 days aboard the station before handing over control to Expedition 2.
The Expedition 1 crew returned to Earth aboard Space Shuttle Discovery on mission STS-102 in March 2001.

disputed: Early ESA press releases (S3) targeted February 2001 for Expedition 2 to take over, whereas actual handover and return occurred in March 2001 (S1, S5, S7); scripts should state the actual March 2001 handover.

S1 notes Russian space agency President Yuriy Semenov disapproved of the name Alpha preferring Beta or Mir 2, while Shepherd insisted on Alpha; scripts should present Alpha as an informal call sign used by the crew.
